alerts.headline: Nature Medicine: ChatGPT Health undertriaged 52% of gold-standard emergencies in structured physician-authored stress test
alerts.detail: Ramaswamy et al. (Nature Medicine, fast-tracked Feb 23 2026) ran the first independent safety evaluation of OpenAI's ChatGPT Health -- tested on the live consumer web interface (gpt-5-mini 'thinking' backbone, 9-11 Jan 2026) -- using 60 clinician-authored vignettes across 21 clinical domains under 16 factorial conditions (960 responses). Performance followed an inverted U-shaped pattern with the most dangerous failures at clinical extremes: 48% failure on emergency conditions (51.6% [33/64] undertriage of gold-standard emergencies such as DKA and impending respiratory failure, directed to 24-48h evaluation instead of the ED) and 35% failure on nonurgent presentations. Anchoring bias was demonstrated: when family/friends minimized symptoms, the probability of a triage shift rose from 3.3% to 13.3% in edge cases (OR 11.7, 95% CI 3.7-36.6; Holm-adjusted p<0.001), mostly toward less-urgent care. Suicide/crisis-safeguard activation was inconsistent and paradoxically inverted relative to clinical severity. This closely matches this protocol's design (physician-authored triage vignettes, factorial/dual-register presentation) and bears directly on the primary endpoint's interpretation (undertriage/critical-miss rate, anchoring-on-benign-explanations, lay-register performance). NOTE: the 2026-08-03 companion alert (Fraile Navarro et al., arXiv 2603.11413) argues this study's forced single-letter (A-D) output format may overstate real-world failure -- see that alert for the methodological debate.

alerts.headline: Preprint challenges Ramaswamy ChatGPT Health undertriage finding: forced-choice exam format, not model capability, drives failure
alerts.detail: Fraile Navarro, Magrabi & Coiera (Macquarie University, arXiv 2603.11413) partially replicated the Nature Medicine ChatGPT Health stress test (Ramaswamy et al., the subject of this library's standing urgent alert) on 5 frontier LLMs (GPT-5.2, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Opus 4.6, Gemini 3 Flash, Gemini 3.1 Pro) across 17 scenarios under two conditions: constrained exam-style forced-choice (A/B/C/D, 1,275 trials) vs naturalistic patient-style free-text messaging (850 trials). Naturalistic interaction improved triage accuracy by 6.4 percentage points (p=0.015); three models scored as low as 0-24% under forced choice but 100% on matched scenarios in free text. This directly bears on the primary endpoint's interpretation: it suggests undertriage/critical-miss rates measured under a forced-choice evaluation format may substantially overstate real-world model failure, and that naturalistic, everyday-language presentation format is itself a major determinant of triage accuracy -- the core dual-register design question this protocol is built around. TWO CAVEATS temper the critique (verified against the Ramaswamy full text): (1) MODEL CONFOUND -- Fraile Navarro tested newer, larger frontier models via API, whereas Ramaswamy tested the actual ChatGPT Health product (gpt-5-mini backbone), so the accuracy gain conflates evaluation format with model capability and is not a clean format-only comparison of the same system; (2) Ramaswamy pre-empted the objection, arguing vignettes are a CONSERVATIVE test because real consumers under-report symptoms and misapply advice, which would compound errors. The two critiques address different axes -- output format vs input quality -- and can both hold, leaving the net real-world effect unresolved. Not yet peer-reviewed (arXiv preprint).

alerts.headline: NOHARM benchmark (ARISE / Stanford & Harvard): physician-authored, harm-weighted evaluation finds up to 22.2% severe-harm potential across 31 LLMs -- closely matches this protocol's own evaluation architecture
alerts.detail: 'First, do NOHARM: towards clinically safe large language models' (Wu, Nateghi Haredasht, ... Goh; ARISE clinical-AI research network, Stanford & Harvard Medical School physicians; arXiv 2512.01241, posted Dec 2025, PMID 41532042) is a physician-authored, harm-weighted clinical-AI safety benchmark. Per the PubMed-indexed record: 100 real primary-care-to-specialist consultation cases across 10 specialties, with 12,747 expert annotations of 4,249 candidate management options by a 29-physician panel. Across 31 LLMs, direct application of AI-generated recommendations carried potential for SEVERE harm in up to 22.2% of cases (95% CI 21.6-22.8%), with errors of omission accounting for 76.6% of errors. Crucially, safety correlated only moderately (r=0.61-0.64) with existing accuracy/knowledge benchmarks -- a model can score well on standard evaluations yet be unsafe -- and the best models slightly exceeded generalist physicians on safety (+9.7%). RELEVANCE: NOHARM's architecture -- physician-authored clinical scenarios with expert-panel, action-level, harm-weighted scoring -- closely parallels this protocol's own physician-authored, harm-weighted evaluation methodology, and its central thesis (clinical safety is a distinct axis from accuracy, requiring explicit measurement) directly supports the protocol's rationale; recommend PI review of the NOHARM harm-scoring rubric for methodological cross-reference. CONTEXT/CAVEAT: the work reached the press only this week via a July 29 2026 Fortune report on an industry dispute (OpenEvidence vs Doximity Ask) over a later, expanded arXiv version that adds a randomized physician-AI teaming study and tests commercial RAG tools; widely-circulated news figures (e.g. '45 LLMs and 4 clinical AI systems', '24.6% severe harm', '>80% omission') come from that secondary coverage/expanded version and differ from the PubMed-indexed abstract cited above -- treat them as unverified pending the specific arXiv version. arXiv preprint (not peer-reviewed); does not resolve either standing alert. UPDATE 2026-08-05 (main session): RESOLVED CAVEAT -- the expanded arXiv version ('...a medical safety benchmark and randomized study of physician and AI teaming on clinical consultations') has now been verified directly from the PI-supplied full PDF: 45 LLMs evaluated (20 notable + 4 clinical RAG tools in primary analyses), severe-harm range 2.9-24.6%, omission >80% of severe errors, 101-physician randomized crossover (AI-assisted 47.3% vs 42.2% conventional; as-treated 52.0%), autograder kappa 0.804 vs inter-physician 0.784, severity weights 1:8:24, 'Do Nothing' floor 37%. Both versions' figures are citable with the version named. Methodological disposition (judging-architecture adoptions) documented in docs/cedars_ramaswamy_nm2026_redraft_plan.md Sec 2.7/3.5.

alerts.headline: New arXiv benchmark (Weilnhammer et al., Microsoft Research/Oxford) tests 15 frontier AI chatbots on one-shot emergency psychiatric triage -- closely parallels this protocol's critical-miss-rate design
alerts.detail: One-shot emergency psychiatric triage across 15 frontier AI chatbots (arXiv 2604.25415, posted 2026-04-28) tested 112 clinical vignettes as realistic single-message disclosures against a 4-level urgency benchmark (A routine / B within-1-week / C within-24-48h / D emergency-now) across 15 frontier chatbots. Emergency under-triage occurred in 5.6% (23/410) of level-D (emergency) trials -- every under-triaged case was reassigned to the next-lower urgency tier (C), a pattern structurally similar to the anchoring-toward-less-urgent-care finding in the standing Ramaswamy Nature Medicine alert. Overall accuracy ranged 42.0-71.8% across models and was lowest for level-B (routine-but-soon) vignettes (19.7%), highest for level-D emergencies (94.3%) -- an inverse U/step pattern distinct from Ramaswamy's inverted-U (which found emergencies and non-urgent cases both as failure extremes). RELEVANCE: this is a new, independently-constructed critical-miss-rate benchmark using single-message (everyday-language-adjacent) disclosures across 15 frontier models -- closely matching this protocol's own primary-endpoint architecture (undertriage/critical-miss rate) and single-message presentation format. Domain is psychiatric emergency triage specifically (not general ED triage), so findings should be read as a parallel/comparator design rather than a direct replication. Not yet peer-reviewed (arXiv preprint); does not resolve any standing alert.

alerts.headline: medRxiv study reusing the standing 60-vignette/16-condition ChatGPT Health harness shows UMLS-CUI prompt augmentation cuts LLM emergency undertriage
alerts.detail: Gokhale et al. (medRxiv, posted Aug 7 2026) apply the same 960-combination clinician-authored vignette harness used in the standing Ramaswamy/Fraile Navarro alerts to test a candidate mitigation: augmenting prompts with UMLS Concept Unique Identifiers. Emergency-case accuracy rose from 73.0% to 80.7% (GPT-4o-mini) and 60.5% to 68.5% (MedGemma 27B), with CUI augmentation reducing anchoring-driven errors. This is the first mitigation-focused study built on the same evaluation architecture as this protocol and the standing undertriage alerts, with direct bearing on interpretation of the primary endpoint and on potential intervention-arm design. RECONCILER CAVEAT (Scite/abstract-verified, 2026-08-15): this is a safety-oriented SHIFT, not a clean win -- UMLS-CUI augmentation reduced under-triage but INCREASED over-triage, with mixed effects on overall accuracy (up for MedGemma 27B, down for GPT-4o-mini); the authors frame the principal value as shifting behavior toward safety-oriented recognition of high-acuity cases rather than uniformly improving accuracy. Not peer-reviewed (openRxiv/medRxiv preprint, posted 2026-08-07).

alerts.headline: MTS-Bench: an LLM emergency-triage safety benchmark reuses the Ramaswamy ChatGPT-Health scenarios (undertriage/dangerous-miss endpoint + anchoring manipulation)
alerts.detail: MTS-Bench (Ravichandran et al., openRxiv preprint 10.64898/2026.08.04.26359651, posted 2026-08-05) adapts the Ramaswamy et al. ChatGPT-Health emergency scenarios -- the same 60-vignette/16-condition lineage this study's standing alerts already track -- and maps them onto the Manchester Triage System (39 cases across all five MTS priority levels; with vs without an objective clinical-data block; with vs without a misleading GP-referral anchoring statement; two genders). The primary endpoint is undertriage on the ordered MTS scale -- a Critical-Miss-Rate-style design closely paralleling this protocol. Findings: GPT-5.1 undertriaged 44.2% of cases (75.0% of Red, 73.4% of Orange), 6 dangerous misses (3.8%); the misleading referral anchor pushed GPT-5.1 to undertriage 8/8 Red cases; adding objective clinical data reduced undertriage. BEARING ON THE TRIAL: a closely design-overlapping emergency-triage safety benchmark now exists on the Ramaswamy scenario base -- the protocol should CITE AND DIFFERENTIATE from it (physician-authored NEW scenarios, patient-facing everyday/lay language, pre-specified dual-register presentation, harm-weighted scoring) to preserve novelty, and may cite the anchoring result as external support for its anchoring/false-reassurance hypotheses. CAVEATS (reconciler, Scite-verified 2026-08-16): (1) preprint, not peer-reviewed; openRxiv is not indexed in US WebSearch, so no independent web corroboration was obtained this run -- verification rests on the full Scite record (title, authors, structured abstract with quantitative results, DOI, date). (2) Partial product evaluation -- authored by the makers of DR. INFO, the agentic retrieval-augmented system reported to outperform GPT-5.1 (both DR. INFO configs 11.5% undertriage / 0 dangerous misses vs GPT-5.1 44.2% / 6), so treat the comparative DR. INFO claim as vendor-reported, not independent. Not resolved -- PI to review and decide on citation/differentiation.

references.title: First, do NOHARM: towards clinically safe large language models

Supports the supporting-strand benchmark-methodology/ESI-ground-truth angle; not peer-reviewed and lower priority (general triage-model engineering rather than physician-authored patient-facing evaluation).

references.title: CARE-Bench: Benchmarking Patient-Facing LLM Triage
references.authors: Hua Y, Na H, Ayubcha C
references.relevance: Source-grounded benchmark evaluating sequential patient-facing triage as a four-label per-turn current-action task (500 cases, 1,059 patient-disclosure prefixes reconstructed from medical dialogue/consultation/follow-up-question sources); 11 models evaluated on 269 held-out rounds under unprompted and minimally prompted open-ended protocols. Unprompted macro-F1 only 31.2-50.4 across models; when the correct action was to ask for more information, only 33.5% of prompted outputs preserved that step, indicating patient-facing triage failures persist after prompting rather than resolving as a simple prompting problem. Directly on this protocol's core question (what action a patient-facing AI should direct given ambiguous/everyday symptom language) though grading uses a fixed LLM mapper rather than physician adjudication -- methodologically adjacent, not a physician-authored evaluation.

references.title: MedMisBench: Measuring Epistemic Resilience of LLMs Under Misleading Medical Context
references.authors: Zhou H, Zou X, Wu J, Wu S, Yu J, Segal BM, et al. (Clifton DA, senior author)
references.relevance: Introduces 'epistemic resilience' (ability to maintain correct medical judgment under adversarial/misleading context) and MedMisBench, a 10,932-item benchmark with 48,889 misleading context-option pairs across medical reasoning, agentic capability, and patient-journey evaluation. Mean accuracy on correctly-answered questions collapses from 71.1% to 38.0% once misleading context is injected (51.5% attack success); authority-framed fabrications and 'spurious anchoring' corruptions are the most damaging injection types. Bears on the search strategy's anchoring/false-reassurance/sycophancy angle -- a lay patient's own framing of symptoms (e.g., minimizing language, a prior benign self-diagnosis volunteered in the message) could function as exactly this kind of misleading context in the everyday-language emergency-recognition scenarios central to this protocol. Not triage-specific; included as ancillary methodology under the clinical-bias filter's anchoring-bias carve-out.

Directly on Topic 1 (Emergency Triage AI Safety); methodologically relevant to this protocol's harm-weighted scoring rationale though it is a framework/position paper, not a physician-authored empirical trial.

references.relevance: Retrospective cohort of 133 pediatric trauma activations at a Level I center (Jan 2023-May 2025) comparing LLM-extracted 'Essential Transcripts' (Whisper-transcribed EMS call audio + named-entity recognition) against human-generated trauma-team pages and injury severity scores. LLM undertriage 4.8% vs human 5.1% (not statistically significant); LLM secondary-endpoint triage accuracy 83.5%, outperforming human clinicians. Prehospital/EMS-communication triage rather than patient-facing conversational triage, but bears directly on this protocol's core undertriage/overtriage axis and on LLM-vs-human-expert comparator methodology.

references.title: When Correct Beliefs Collapse: Epistemic Resilience of LLMs under Clinical Pressure
references.authors: Xiao B, Tian X, Song X, Wang H, Song G, Zhao S, Qin B
references.relevance: Harbin Institute of Technology group introduces MED-STRESS, a stress-test framework measuring belief stability of LLMs under escalating multi-turn clinical pressure (patient pushback/challenge). Bears on the search strategy's anchoring/false-reassurance/sycophancy carve-out: a lay patient minimizing or reframing symptoms functions as exactly this kind of pressure in the everyday-language emergency-recognition scenarios central to this protocol. Not triage-specific; included as ancillary methodology under the same rationale as the already-captured MedMisBench entry.

Directly on the Core Question Anchor: shows frontier-model clinical knowledge does not reliably transmit through lay/conversational human-AI interaction, the mechanism this protocol's dual-register design probes. A Publisher Correction (10.1038/s41591-026-04404-8, April 2026) fixed a y-axis mislabel in Figure 2a only; does not affect reported findings.

Bears on Topic 1 (emergency triage AI safety) and the consumer-product-name search angle for a vulnerable patient-facing population; predates this protocol's 2026-08-02 seed sweep but was not previously captured.

references.title: A clinically validated framework for auditing AI chatbot behavior in mental health interactions
references.authors: Weilnhammer V, Hou KYC, Luettgau L, Summerfield C, Dolan R, Nour MM
references.relevance: UCL/Oxford/UK AI Security Institute team (same group behind the standing 2026-08-06 psychiatric one-shot triage alert) introduces SIM-VAIL, an automated multi-turn evaluation framework that simulates users with specific psychiatric vulnerabilities and adversarial conversational intents (e.g., pressuring the chatbot to downplay symptoms or endorse risky actions) against 9 frontier consumer chatbots (Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok, Llama). Across 810 conversations / 90,000+ turn-level ratings, concerning vulnerability-amplifying behavior was widespread across nearly all simulated user profiles, reduced but not eliminated in newer models; automated scoring showed substantial agreement with clinician raters. Methodologically close to this protocol's own harm-graded, multi-model behavioral-audit architecture (systematic multi-turn adversarial probing scored against clinical risk dimensions), though the domain is psychiatric conversational risk rather than one-shot ESI-style triage disposition. No PMID yet (published 2026-08-07; likely not yet PubMed-indexed).

references.authors: Souza LL, de Oliveira YCN, Campos da Costa LC, Silva Filho JAAD, de Souza ATF, Mourão VG, Neves Dantas RA, Botarelli FR, Ribeiro KRB

references.title: This Treatment Works, Right? Evaluating LLM Sensitivity to Patient Question Framing in Medical QA
references.authors: Yun HS, Kapoor G, Mackert M, Kouzy R, Xu W, Li JJ, Wallace BC
references.relevance: Controlled RAG medical-QA study: 6,614 query pairs varying patient question framing (positive vs. negative) and language style (technical vs. plain) grounded in clinical-trial abstracts, evaluated across 8 LLMs; positively- and negatively-framed pairs produced significantly more contradictory conclusions than same-framing pairs. Direct evidence on the Core Question Anchor's lay-language/register-effect dimension.

references.title: MIRA: A Bilingual Benchmark for Medical Information Response Audit
references.authors: Xu M, Yang Q, Wang Q, Dai X, Wu W, Gao C
references.relevance: Bilingual controlled benchmark (4,320 prompts built from 60 medically-reviewed low-risk health questions) testing whether LLMs give comparable medical information across user-side language/register/health-literacy signals; identifies 'Differential Information Dilution' -- across 5 mainstream LLMs, responses to low-health-literacy phrasing consistently omitted more key information and offered fewer concrete next steps. Direct evidence on the Core Question Anchor's health-literacy dimension.

references.title: SymptomAI: Toward a Conversational AI Agent for Everyday Symptom Assessment
references.authors: Breda J, Yousif F, Hawkins B, Cotoi M, Liu M, Luo R, Chen PC, Schaekermann M, Schmidgall S, Liu X, et al.
references.relevance: Google/Fitbit conversational symptom-assessment agent randomized to 13,917 real-world users comparing 5 AI-agent conversational strategies against independent clinicians reviewing the same dialogue; agentic strategies running a dedicated symptom interview before diagnosing significantly outperformed clinician comparators (OR 2.56, p<0.001) on differential-diagnosis accuracy. Large real-world physician-comparator study directly on the Core Question Anchor's conversational/everyday-language symptom-description dimension.

references.title: Triage Performance Across Large Language Models, ChatGPT, and Untrained Doctors in Emergency Medicine: Comparative Study
references.authors: Masanneck L, Schmidt L, Seifert A, et al.
references.relevance: Comparative study (Manchester Triage System): 124 case vignettes triaged by untrained doctors, several LLMs (raw GPT-4, Llama 3 70B, Gemini 1.5, Mixtral 8x7b) and ChatGPT (GPT-3.5/GPT-4) against a professional-rater consensus gold standard, scored by quadratic-weighted Cohen kappa. GPT-4-based ChatGPT (kappa 0.67) matched untrained ED doctors (0.68) and beat GPT-3.5 (0.54), but none reached professional-rater level; LLMs/ChatGPT tended to OVER-triage whereas untrained doctors UNDER-triaged, and LLM second-opinion did not significantly improve untrained doctors' triage. Direct LLM-vs-human emergency-triage comparator bearing on Topics 1 & 3 (over/undertriage endpoints, physician-consensus grading). Surfaced via the digital.health/journals coverage expansion (JMIR); previously uncaptured.

references.title: Multi-Evidence Clinical Reasoning With Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Emergency Triage: Retrospective Evaluation Study
references.authors: Wong HS, Wong TK
references.relevance: Hong Kong ED physicians' dual-source RAG system (grounded in the Hong Kong Accident & Emergency Triage Guidelines plus 3,000 retrieved past ED encounters) evaluated retrospectively against triage-nurse ground truth: mean QWK 0.902 / accuracy 0.802 vs. prompt-only baseline LLM QWK 0.801 / accuracy 0.542, reducing 3-group overtriage from 28.8% (baseline LLM) to 12.7% while holding undertriage at 1.3%. Clinician decision-support tool rather than patient-facing lay-language AI, but directly on Topic 1's undertriage/overtriage measurement architecture and a useful guideline-grounding comparator for the protocol's own triage-accuracy metrics.

references.title: MedPI: Evaluating AI Systems in Medical Patient-facing Interactions
references.authors: Fajardo V D, Proniakin O, Gruber VE, Marinescu R
references.relevance: High-dimensional benchmark for LLM patient-clinician conversations: synthetic EHR-grounded 'AI Patients' with memory/affect are interviewed by 9 flagship models (Claude Opus 4.1, Claude Sonnet 4, MedGemma, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Llama 3.3 70B, GPT-5, GPT-OSS-120B, o3, Grok-4) across 366 AI patients / 7,097 conversations, scored on a 105-dimension ACGME-competency-aligned rubric by calibrated committee-based AI Judges; low performance concentrated in differential-diagnosis dimensions. Directly on Topic 2's evaluation-framework/accreditation-aligned-rubric architecture for patient-facing AI, though the 'physicians' in the grading loop are AI Judges rather than human physicians -- a methodological point of contrast with this protocol's physician-authored design.

references.title: AIPatient Arena: EHR-grounded evaluation of large language models in end-to-end clinical consultation workflows
references.authors: Niu J, Yu H, Wang W, Dai G, He J, Li X, Liang Z, Lin X, So KCY, Yan BYP, Wing YK, Xing Y, Ma X, Fan L
references.relevance: Shandong University / Chinese University of Hong Kong EHR-grounded evaluation framework integrating patient-specific knowledge graphs into multi-turn LLM consultations, scored across 8 clinical-competence dimensions on a primary cohort of 437 patients plus two out-of-distribution validation cohorts (n=119, n=67); models scored well on interview questioning and professionalism (4.4-5.0/5) but weak on handling ambiguous patient responses (2.6-3.3/5), information coverage (2.1-3.0/5), and diagnostic accuracy/reasoning (2.6-3.6/5). Supporting-strand hit on Topic 2's rubric-based patient-facing AI evaluation methodology; general clinical consultation rather than ED-triage-specific.

references.title: Reducing Under-Triage Risk in Large Language Model Based Clinical Triage Using UMLS-CUI Augmentation
references.authors: Gokhale R, Kukreja M, Kumar N, Gourab K
references.relevance: Reuses the same 60 clinician-authored vignette x 16 factorial-condition harness (960 combinations) as the standing Ramaswamy/Fraile Navarro benchmark to test whether augmenting LLM prompts with UMLS Concept Unique Identifiers reduces undertriage; emergency-case accuracy improved from 73.0% to 80.7% (GPT-4o-mini) and 60.5% to 68.5% (MedGemma 27B), with CUI augmentation reducing susceptibility to anchoring statements. First mitigation-focused study built on the same evaluation architecture as this protocol and the standing undertriage alerts -- flagged as urgent alert.

references.title: SycoEval-EM: Sycophancy Evaluation of Large Language Models in Simulated Clinical Encounters for Emergency Care
references.authors: Peng D, Wang Y, Schoeffler A, Preiksaitis C, Rose C
references.relevance: Multi-agent adversarial-persuasion framework testing sycophancy/acquiescence in 20 LLMs across 1,875 simulated emergency-medicine encounters built on Choosing Wisely low-value-care scenarios; acquiescence rates ranged 0-100% and were highest for imaging requests (38.8%). Direct evidence on the false-reassurance/anchoring/sycophancy failure mode named in the search strategy's Topic 1.

references.title: Iterative Multidisciplinary Development and Evaluation of a Patient-Facing Social Determinants of Health Chatbot Using Synthetic Data Simulation: Mixed Methods Study
references.authors: Maw AM, Lupi A, Johnson-Koenke R, Coats H, Zhou L, Li B, Mitchell J, Kotz A, Plasek J, Goss F
references.relevance: Develops and applies a 10-item multidisciplinary evaluation rubric (accuracy, trustworthiness, empathy; binary met/not-met scoring) for grading a patient-facing chatbot's synthetic-scenario outputs before clinical deployment. Methodological example of clinician-authored rubric-based grading of patient-facing AI -- the Topic 2 evaluation-framework strand of this protocol.

references.title: Locally Deployable Small Language Models for Emergency Department Decision Support: A Systematic Benchmark of Fine-Tuning Strategies
references.authors: Zhang Q, Guo Y, Gong Y
references.relevance: Benchmarks 8 open-source small language models (zero-shot, prefix-tuning, LoRA, full fine-tuning) against Claude Haiku 4.5/Sonnet 4.5 baselines on 2,083 MIMIC-IV-ED cases for triage-level prediction, specialist-referral recommendation, and diagnosis prediction; LoRA-tuned SLMs outperformed the commercial baselines on triage-level prediction. Clinically-oriented benchmark methodology relevant to the trial's evaluation architecture.

references.title: MTS-Bench: A Manchester Triage System Benchmark for Language Model Triage Safety
references.authors: Ravichandran S, Romano M, Corga da Silva R, et al.
references.relevance: HIGH design overlap. MTS-Bench adapts the Ramaswamy et al. ChatGPT-Health emergency scenarios -- the same 60-vignette/16-condition lineage this study's standing alerts already track -- and maps them onto the Manchester Triage System: 39 emergency cases spanning all five MTS priority levels, each tested with and without an objective clinical-data block (vitals/exam/labs) and permuted across two genders (156 prompts/condition), and with vs without a misleading GP-referral anchoring statement (312 prompts/system). Primary endpoint is undertriage on the ordered MTS scale -- a Critical-Miss-Rate-style design closely paralleling this protocol. GPT-5.1 undertriaged 44.2% of cases (95% CI 36.7-52.1), including 75.0% of Red and 73.4% of Orange presentations, with 6 dangerous misses (3.8%); prepending the misleading referral anchor drove GPT-5.1 to undertriage 8/8 Red cases; adding objective clinical data reduced undertriage. Bears on this trial: a closely design-overlapping emergency-triage safety benchmark now exists on the Ramaswamy scenario base -- the protocol should cite and differentiate (physician-authored NEW scenarios, patient-facing everyday/lay language, pre-specified dual-register presentation, harm-weighted scoring) to preserve novelty, and may cite the anchoring result as external support for its anchoring/false-reassurance hypotheses. CAVEATS (reconciler, Scite-verified 2026-08-16; openRxiv preprint not indexed in US WebSearch, so no independent web corroboration this run): (1) preprint, not peer-reviewed (posted 2026-08-05); (2) partial product evaluation -- authored by the makers of DR. INFO, the agentic retrieval-augmented system it reports as dramatically outperforming GPT-5.1 (both DR. INFO configs 11.5% undertriage / 0 dangerous misses vs GPT-5.1 44.2% / 6), so treat the comparative DR. INFO claim as vendor-reported rather than independent.

references.title: AI-assisted rheumatology triage changes with referral framing
references.authors: Omar M, Naffaa ME, Agbareia R, et al.
references.relevance: Close methodological parallel to this protocol's register-manipulation design. Controlled, physician-validated experiment: 30 physician-authored rheumatology vignettes, each independently rephrased 3x (90 variants), tested across 5 LLMs (Anthropic/Google/OpenAI) under 9 dimensions (demographics, clinical context, communication framing), 57 contextual modifications, 4 personas, 5 reps/cell = 200,000+ queries; 16 clinical fields graded vs physician-validated ground truth (Fleiss kappa 0.92). Baseline concordance was high (0.869) but readily disrupted by HOW the case was framed/worded, NOT by demographics: 'anxious' framing tripled psychological (vs organic) attribution (13.1% vs 4.5%; OR 3.2 vs stoic framing), risking relabeling organic disease as functional; a dismissive clinician anchor in the referral note significantly reduced acuity concordance (vignette-level p=0.01), mainly by downgrading urgency; race/ethnicity, SES and language barrier produced no detectable effect. Authors recommend separating objective clinical evidence from interpretive framing and treating urgency and psychological attribution as auditable safety signals. SETTING CAVEAT: this is rheumatology REFERRAL triage (clinician-facing referral notes determining specialist-access speed), not emergency or patient-facing everyday-language triage -- but the physician-authored-vignette + controlled-rephrasing + urgency-endpoint methodology, and the finding that framing beats demographics, directly parallel and support this study's register-sensitivity hypothesis.

references.title: Sociodemographic bias in LLMs' clinical decision-making for dizziness
references.authors: Tessler I, Omar M, Wolfovitz A, et al.
references.relevance: Cross-randomized in-silico vignette study of LLM recommendation robustness in an emergency-department presentation: 100 synthetic ED dizziness cases built on established diagnostic frameworks (TiTrATE, SAEM GRACE-3, Barany Society criteria), each tested neutral + 33 sociodemographic descriptor variants (34 total), across 12 instruction-tuned LLMs, 10 reps/cell = 2,040,000 responses. Models answered five binary decisions including TRIAGE DISPOSITION, neuroimaging, and mental-health referral. Sociodemographic descriptors shifted recommendations, largest for mental-health referral in diagnostically ambiguous cases (lower referral for Black transgender women -12.2 pp [95% CI -14.0 to -10.3], Black patients experiencing homelessness -9.1 pp, homelessness -7.7 pp; +4.0 pp neuroimaging for low-income descriptors); disparities attenuated when vignettes carried clearer diagnostic information. Bears on Topic 1: descriptor-sensitivity/robustness of LLM emergency triage-disposition recommendations, in a classic can't-miss ED presentation (dizziness masking posterior stroke); reinforces that structured/objective clinical detail mitigates input-framing effects -- complementary to the Omar 2026 finding that framing outweighs demographics (overlapping Mount Sinai / Klang group).

references.title: Accuracy of Chatbot-Based Health Advice Related to Traumatic Dental Injuries: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
references.authors: Tewari N, Kidwai AA, Wadhwani E, et al.
references.relevance: Systematic review + meta-analysis (Cochrane Handbook + CHART reporting tool, OSF-registered) of contemporary consumer chatbots answering patient questions about emergency care of traumatic dental injuries -- a time-critical presentation (e.g., avulsion has a short replantation window). 10 studies (2024-2025), 7 chatbots; pooled accuracy 65% (95% CI 52-78) for ChatGPT-3.5, 79% (61-93) for ChatGPT-4.0, 70% (60-79) for Gemini, with high heterogeneity (I2 ~86-89%). Authors conclude accuracy is only moderate and highly question-dependent and explicitly caution these figures 'should not be interpreted as evidence of clinical reliability, as even limited inaccuracies in emergency dental trauma advice may contribute to delayed or inappropriate management and adverse outcomes.' Topic 2 / patient-facing-AI: consumer-chatbot advice accuracy and its safety ceiling for an urgent, everyday-language health question.

references.title: Deployment protocol and base model jointly determine residual risk in rule-based clinical LLM supervision
references.authors: Wu K, Nagori A, Kamaleswaran R, et al.
references.relevance: Evaluates a five-gate 'sentinel' rule-based supervisor over five models (Qwen 7B, Llama 8B, Meditron 7B, Gemma 4, Sonnet 4.5) on two clinical safety benchmarks under handoff-on/off protocols; residual safety depended on both deployment protocol and base model (strict violation rates 1.5-49.5%; handoff-off residual risk 0-50%). A multisite extension (Llama 70B, N=2935 encounter-derived scenarios) and HealthBench Hard (N=1000) reached ~0% deploy-violation under supervision. KEY physician-evaluation point for this study: a clinician-adjudication pilot (n=50) separated automated safety-rule compliance from clinical adequacy -- of 20 intercepted outputs none were rated harmful but ALL were flagged for missing critical information, while 5/30 ALLOWED outputs were rated potentially harmful (clinical-reasoning errors beyond the sentinel's scope). Supports the protocol's core thesis that physician-authored/adjudicated evaluation surfaces harms that automated compliance metrics miss. CAVEAT: preprint (Research Square), Scite-verified metadata/abstract; not peer-reviewed and no independent web corroboration this run.

references.title: Large language models exhibit greater diagnostic anchoring than physicians in a forced-choice vignette study
references.authors: Sheppert A, Shen C, Geissal E, et al.
references.relevance: Head-to-head LLM-vs-physician test of the anchoring failure mode that is central to this protocol (anchoring on a plausible benign explanation / false reassurance). Forced-choice ranking over 9 pairs of internal-medicine outpatient vignettes, each pair an anchored version (a PATIENT STATEMENT suggesting a plausible-but-unlikely diagnosis) vs a matched control; 20 PGY1-3 IM residents + 5 attendings (225 responses) vs 8 LLMs (144 outputs). Primary endpoint = proportion ranking the anchor first: LLMs 55.6% (40/72) vs residents 21.2% (17/80) vs attendings 10.0% (2/20); LLMs' odds of ranking the anchor first were ~4x physicians' (vs residents OR 3.94, 95% CI 2.32-7.33; vs attendings OR 4.07, 2.47-7.21; both P<0.001), and LLMs put the anchor in the top-5 in 97.2% of outputs (vs 67.5%/65.0%). Directly supports the study's premise that a lay-phrased benign cue can distort AI reasoning more than clinicians'. Also bears on the standing Fraile Navarro alert (which argues forced-choice exam format inflates LLM triage failures): here, within the SAME forced-choice paradigm, LLMs anchor substantially more than humans, i.e. the format does not equalize them. CAVEAT: internal-medicine differential-diagnosis ranking, not emergency triage-acuity or a harm-weighted endpoint; authors call for open-ended real-world follow-up.

references.title: Clinical safety of large language model responses to matched patient-language and clinician-language Turkish obstetric and gynecologic triage prompts: a model-blinded paired-scenario study
references.authors: Ada O, Dagli U, Bilen E, et al.
references.journal: European Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology and Reproductive Biology
references.relevance: Direct methodological parallel to this protocol's DUAL-REGISTER design: 30 obstetric/gynecologic triage scenarios presented in MATCHED patient-language vs clinician-language (Turkish) formats to 4 LLMs, with 5 specialists blindly rating 240 responses (1,200 ratings) on a Global Clinical Confidence Score (GCCS 0-2) plus five secondary safety/appropriateness scales, analyzed with ordinal GEE adjusted for model and evaluator. Result is a NOTABLE NULL/CONTRASTING finding: clinically reliable responses (GCCS=2) were 89.3% clinician-language vs 91.3% patient-language, and lay phrasing was NOT significantly associated with overall confidence (cumulative OR 0.78, 95% CI 0.57-1.06; p=0.115); if anything patient-language had fewer unsafe (GCCS=0) ratings (OR 0.66, p=0.031; McNemar ns) and higher evaluator-level triage-appropriateness and clinical-applicability after FDR correction. This is important for methods differentiation and interpretation: it is a specialty (OB/GYN), specialist-RATED (not physician-authored patient-facing everyday-language) triage study whose register-invariance CONTRASTS with the register-sensitivity reported for framing (Omar 2026) and symptom-report quality (Reis 2026); the protocol should engage it directly. design_overlap flagged true (matched lay-vs-clinician paired-scenario triage-safety design). NOT raised as an urgent alert: null result, single specialty, expert-rated rather than an ED patient-facing critical-miss benchmark.

references.title: AI-generated patient instructions as safety-critical communication: a provisional evidence-informed framework for clinical deployment
references.authors: Gwóźdź-Broczkowska A.
references.relevance: Narrative/interpretative review that reframes AI-generated patient-facing instructions (discharge summaries, medication explanations, portal messages, plain-language materials) as a SAFETY-CRITICAL informatics intervention rather than a readability tool: patients may act on fluent, incomplete, or contextually unsafe AI text without the clinical knowledge to detect the error, and physician/pharmacist review of such outputs has found omissions, inaccuracies, newly-introduced actions, medication problems, and potentially harmful safety issues (especially in complex discharge contexts). Proposes a seven-domain safety framework -- factual accuracy, clinical completeness, actionability, medication clarity, ESCALATION and safety-netting, health-literacy alignment, and accountability/auditability -- to support implementation, local evaluation, and reviewer assessment, and calls for human verification, traceability, equity testing, and post-deployment monitoring for high-risk outputs. Bears on this protocol's patient-facing-AI-safety framing: the escalation/safety-netting domain is precisely the mechanism against false reassurance / failure to advise urgent care, health-literacy alignment is the everyday-/lay-language dimension, and the finding that physician/pharmacist review catches harms readability metrics miss echoes the study's physician-authored-evaluation rationale. CAVEAT: single-author narrative review proposing a PROVISIONAL framework (explicitly not a formal consensus guideline and not an empirical evaluation); PubMed-verified metadata only -- too recent for Scite indexing this run, so no Scite editorialNotices/citation check was available.

references.title: ED-triage-agent: a multi-agent framework for human-in-the-loop emergency triage
references.authors: Sharma K, Sivadas H, Edwards C, et al.
references.relevance: Multi-agent LLM emergency-triage architecture (ED-Triage-Agent / ETA): five specialised agents orchestrated via LangGraph, grounded in the ESI Implementation Handbook v4 by retrieval-augmented generation, calibrated on 30 ESI Handbook Practice Cases. Two-phase design directly relevant to this protocol's endpoints: Phase 1 produces a provisional ESI-scaled acuity signal from SYMPTOM-ONLY data for pre-vital queue prioritisation (deciding who is seen next before vital signs exist -- an information-incomplete, symptom-text setting close to patient-facing lay-language triage); Phase 2 gives a criterion-linked ESI recommendation once vitals are available. On the external TRIAGEAGENT benchmark: Phase 1 76.39% exact-match (quadratic-weighted kappa 0.8787) with 95.52% high-priority sensitivity; Phase 2 87.04% exact-match (kappa 0.9090) with 0.00% significant over-triage and 0.46% significant under-triage (97.22% of misclassifications within +/-1 ESI level), versus 10.00% significant under-triage for a chain-of-thought baseline. Bears on Topic 1 (ESI-scaled undertriage/overtriage and high-priority sensitivity as safety endpoints; the CoT-vs-agentic contrast quantifies architecture-driven undertriage). CAVEAT: technical-feasibility study on standardized ESI Handbook / benchmark cases, not real ED data or clinician users; the authors state clinical utility, safety, and workflow integration remain to be established by prospective validation. Verified via PubMed metadata (source pubmed-verified); DOI not yet in Scite's index this run (brand-new), so no Scite editorialNotices check -- none can exist for a day-old article.

references.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI)-Assisted Self-Diagnosis and the Patient-Physician Relationship: Mixed Methods Study of Calibration, Participation, and Trust
references.authors: Ding W, Wang J.
references.relevance: Exploratory sequential mixed-methods study (48 semistructured interviews + 546-person web survey, Chinese adults who had used generative AI to interpret symptoms within the prior 6-12 months) of how consumer generative-AI self-diagnosis is folded into real-world care-seeking -- the exact patient-facing, everyday-language behavior at the heart of this protocol's core question. Qualitatively, AI-assisted self-diagnosis was used in a 'prediagnostic gray zone for preliminary orientation, INFORMAL TRIAGE, and interim self-management,' helping patients appraise illness severity, prepare for consultations, ask questions, and understand physicians' reasoning. Quantitatively, perceived AI quality was associated with calibrated illness appraisal (beta 0.57, 95% CI 0.49-0.64) which was associated with greater patient participation (beta 0.35), and with diagnosis validation/comprehension which were associated with higher trust in physicians; authors frame AI as an informational intermediary rather than something that undermines medical authority. Bears on the everyday-language / self-triage / illness-severity-appraisal dimension: characterizes how patients actually use whatever consumer chatbot is at hand to gauge whether symptoms need care. CAVEAT: self-report, purposive/convenience sampling in China, correlational (mediation) design -- it measures perceptions, participation, and trust, NOT triage accuracy, undertriage, or harm. Verified via PubMed metadata (source pubmed-verified); DOI not yet in Scite's index this run (brand-new).

references.title: Prospective evaluation of a large language model clinical decision support system in the emergency department
references.authors: Leibovitch L, Ahituv A, Gorenshtein A, et al.
references.relevance: One of the few PROSPECTIVE in-ED evaluations of an LLM clinical decision support system (Topic 1). DECIDE-AI stage 1 evaluation of SHAKED (a CDSS built on multiple LLMs) in a tertiary emergency department: 1,138 patients over 4 weeks across two parallel units (one using SHAKED, one routine). Findings: clinical adoption declined from 68% to 30% (workload-sensitive disengagement, OR 0.72 per shift hour, 95% CI 0.62-0.83); physicians preferred SHAKED for radiology consultations (OR 2.98, 95% CI 1.58-5.63); NO adverse events, and expert review rated 99/100 sampled outputs clinically appropriate; ED length of stay unchanged (4.9 h both wings, p=0.99); a non-significant trend toward shorter consultation cycle time (-9.4 min, p=0.077). The authors conclude that sustained clinician engagement -- not algorithmic accuracy -- may be the key barrier to effective clinical AI in EDs, and that the results inform randomized trial design but 'do not justify clinical deployment at this stage' (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06902675). Complements the Taylor (NEJM AI) implementation study and Cotte (NEJM AI) real-world study in the real-world-ED-evaluation strand. CAVEAT: clinician-facing ED decision support (not patient-facing / lay-language triage), single tertiary center, stage-1 feasibility. Verified via PubMed metadata (source pubmed-verified); not yet in Scite's index (brand-new 2026-08-19).

references.title: Patient-Facing AI System for Symptom Guidance Using Simulated Encounters and Physician Review: Analytical Validation Study
references.authors: Patwardhan A, Verma N, Barman P, et al.
references.relevance: CLOSEST design parallel to this protocol surfaced to date: a physician-panel-adjudicated, PATIENT-FACING symptom-guidance triage-safety validation with prespecified undertriage/overtriage endpoints. Predeployment analytical validation of a locked configuration of Verily Health's Personal Health Assistant (PHA), an LLM-enabled patient-facing symptom-guidance tool: 772 synthetic cases built from published TELEPHONE-TRIAGE protocols plus persona-based, LLM-assisted case generation, each with a clinical vignette, structured history, and a simulated MULTITURN patient conversation; a panel of 5 independent physicians (BLINDED to PHA outputs) set case-level level-of-care ground truth via prespecified plurality/tie-handling rules. Against prespecified criteria: urgent undertriage 6.9% (95% CI 4.6-9.8; criterion <5% -- NOT met), nonurgent undertriage 18.4% (95% CI 14.2-23.2; criterion <15% -- NOT met), overtriage 11.0% (95% CI 8.0-14.7; criterion <30% -- met); undertriage was identified as the principal performance gap. This shares the protocol's physician-panel-adjudicated, patient-facing, undertriage/overtriage-endpoint design and telephone-triage-protocol case basis -- the study should CITE AND DIFFERENTIATE on the axes that keep it distinct: physician-AUTHORED NEW scenarios (vs synthetic/persona-generated), pre-specified DUAL-REGISTER lay-vs-clinician presentation, and HARM-WEIGHTED / Critical-Miss-Rate primary scoring. Flagged design_overlap:true and surfaced to the PI. NOT auto-escalated to a formal urgent alert: it is a predeployment analytical validation of a single commercial product on SYNTHETIC cases and simulated conversations (JMIR Formative Research), lacking dual-register and harm-weighting -- but it is the strongest design match yet and the PI may wish to escalate. Verified via PubMed metadata + Scite (Scite holds the preprint record 'Validation of a Patient-Facing AI System for Symptom Guidance: A Simulation Study With Physician Review'; authors Patwardhan/Verma/Barman; no editorialNotices / retraction).

references.title: Safety and security of large language models in healthcare
references.authors: Clusmann J, Freyer O, Ostermann M, et al.
references.relevance: Nature systematic review of the safety and security of clinical large language models -- a landmark-venue framing reference for this protocol's LLM-safety context. Maps security hazards to the development stages of clinical AI systems (design, data, model, inference, environment); identifies safety layers from core optimization objectives, knowledge integrity, and alignment through interaction with humans and systems; classifies threats by current clinical relevance; and surveys mitigation techniques with the corresponding stakeholder responsibilities. Broader than triage, but directly relevant to the study's safety rationale and to the failure surfaces (alignment, human-interaction, inference-time manipulation) that a patient-facing emergency-triage AI must withstand. CAVEAT: comprehensive review across all clinical LLM use, not triage-specific. Verified via PubMed metadata (source pubmed-verified); not yet in Scite's index (brand-new 2026-08-19).

references.title: The Reliability of Human Evaluation of Large Language Models in Health Care Settings: Scoping Review
references.authors: Yang E, Ko S, Woo H.
references.relevance: PRISMA-ScR scoping review (71 studies, Jan 2016-Jul 2025) mapping how HUMAN EVALUATION of clinical LLM reliability is actually operationalized -- methodologically foundational for this protocol's physician-authored-evaluation design. Six reliability indicators recur (accuracy, relevance, completeness, clarity, safety, consistency); clinical-domain evaluations emphasized guideline concordance, internal consistency, and structural coherence, whereas public-health evaluations emphasized understandability, harm potential, and repeat-response consistency; single-specialty clinicians were the most common evaluators, evaluator panels were generally 5 or fewer members, and 5-point Likert scales with researcher-defined rubrics were the common approach. Key limitations across the field: evaluator subjectivity, nonstandardized indicators, and limited evaluation scope/settings -- leading the authors to conclude human LLM evaluation is insufficiently standardized and to call for domain-specific standardized frameworks (indicator definitions, judgment criteria, evaluator guidance, and procedures). Directly informs the study's rubric design, evaluator-panel construction, and indicator standardization. CAVEAT: a scoping review of evaluation METHODOLOGY, not an evaluation of triage performance. references.title: A scoping review on the mental health harms of LLM-based chatbots
references.authors: Diel A, Torous J, Cuijpers P, et al.
references.relevance: PRISMA-based scoping review (N=3,137 records screened across ACM, IEEE, PubMed, Science.gov, Google Scholar; 119 included) synthesizing the documented and hypothesized mental-health harms of consumer LLM-based chatbots -- a patient-facing-AI-safety reference in a priority journal (npj Digital Medicine; senior authors incl. Torous and Cuijpers). Five harm categories: (1) conceptual works citing chatbot limitations (hallucinations, SYCOPHANCY, bias), data-security issues, and risks in severe/high-risk psychiatric cases (e.g., suicide, psychosis); (2) VIGNETTE studies showing LLM chatbots respond INAPPROPRIATELY to mental-health queries relative to clinical standards; (3) cognitive overreliance associated with reduced cognitive/academic performance; (4) problematic use (emotional/social dependency, withdrawal) correlating with mental-health symptoms; (5) 'AI psychosis' -- chatbots reinforcing/validating delusional beliefs. Bears on this protocol's patient-facing-AI-safety and CRISIS-SAFEGUARDS dimensions: the finding that chatbots mishandle high-risk psychiatric queries against clinical standards parallels the study's concern with false reassurance / failure to recognize emergencies in everyday-language interaction (cf. the standing Weilnhammer emergency-psychiatric-triage alert and the Ramaswamy inconsistent-crisis-safeguards finding). CAVEAT: a scoping review of mental-health harms specifically (not emergency symptom/disposition triage), mixing hypothetical/conceptual with empirical harms. references.authors: Li Q, Sun Y, Ju X, Cui J.
references.relevance: Guideline-informed cross-sectional TRIAGE-SAFETY evaluation of patient-facing chatbots -- directly on this protocol's endpoints (red-flag/urgency RECOGNITION and appropriate patient ACTION), in a single symptom domain. 36 English simulated patient questions across 6 nipple-discharge modules x 6 commonly-used AI chatbots = 216 first-turn responses; two reviewers scored each against a guideline-informed reference standard + structured checklist (DISCERN, red-flag recognition, actionability, guideline concordance, error typing), with a senior third-reviewer adjudicating. references.title: Subgroup Differences in Agreement Between an Algorithm-Guided Large Language Model and Routine Emergency Department Triage
references.authors: Halıcı A, Cesur E, Çelik F.
references.relevance: ED-triage agreement study whose headline is SUBGROUP UNDERTRIAGE -- directly on Topic 1's undertriage-as-safety-endpoint and the fairness/equity dimension. Retrospective, 1,960 adult ED visits with complete triage data; a standardized prompt (age, sex, chief complaint, comorbidities, systolic/diastolic BP, heart rate, SpO2, temperature, GCS) had the LLM assign one category in a 5-level ESI-based system, compared against routine ED triage. Overall: 71.3% five-level accuracy, substantial agreement (quadratic-weighted kappa 0.824); urgent-vs-non-urgent AUC 0.768, sensitivity 0.630, specificity 0.906. Lower-acuity (potential UNDERTRIAGE) discordance 9.8% and higher-acuity (overtriage) 18.9% -- and, crucially, discordance was NON-UNIFORM across subgroups: lower-acuity/undertriage assignments vs routine triage were more frequent in OLDER ADULTS, TRAUMA, and DIABETES, while infectious presentations showed the highest concordance. That systematic subgroup undertriage pattern is a named safety-failure-mode / equity finding that bears on the protocol's undertriage endpoint and its bias-across-subgroups concern. CAVEAT: the LLM was fed structured clinical data + vitals (a clinician-data decision-support comparison, NOT patient-facing lay-language free text), and the authors are explicit that routine triage was an operational comparator, not a gold standard -- so results reflect agreement with local practice, not definitive accuracy or safety; prospective outcome validation is required. design_overlap FALSE (structured-data agreement study, not a patient-facing dual-register physician-authored eval); NOT alerted. references.title: Can Large Language Models Preserve Diagnostic Accuracy Despite Patient Self-Diagnosis and Framing Bias in Hypothetical Upper-Extremity Scenarios?
references.authors: Jaarsma EH, Ring D, Wickman J, Drost A.
references.relevance: A named-failure-mode (ANCHORING / patient self-diagnosis / framing-bias) study that provides a CONTRASTING NULL to the standing Sheppert anchoring finding (added 2026-08-17), which reported LLMs anchor on a lay-stated cue far more than physicians. Here ChatGPT (GPT-5) evaluated 180 randomized hypothetical vignettes across five common upper-extremity conditions (de Quervain tendinopathy, rotator cuff tendinopathy, lateral epicondylitis, trigger digit, trapeziometacarpal arthritis), each vignette carrying randomized patient characteristics, characteristic-vs-VAGUE symptom descriptions, and a PATIENT SELF-DIAGNOSIS (correct / plausible alternative / common misconception). Result: the model identified the intended diagnosis in 165/180 (92%); accuracy was UNAFFECTED by the patient's self-diagnosis (higher for characteristic than vague symptoms; lower for de Quervain); it deviated from the patient's proposed diagnosis in 117/180 (65%), of which 104 (89%) appropriately aligned with the intended diagnosis, and it was more likely to disregard patient-provided diagnoses that did not match the intended one. Authors conclude GPT-5 showed LIMITED susceptibility to the anchoring/confirmation/acquiescence biases known to affect human reasoning and could support debiasing / correcting patient misconceptions. Bears on the protocol's anchoring/false-reassurance and lay-language self-diagnosis dimensions, and is valuable for balance: the library now holds both an anchoring-VULNERABLE result (Sheppert, forced-choice IM DDx, LLMs anchor > physicians) and this anchoring-RESISTANT result (single newest-model, open-ended DDx). CAVEAT: condition-specific upper-extremity MUSCULOSKELETAL diagnostic accuracy (NOT emergency/urgency triage or a harm-weighted endpoint), hypothetical vignettes, single model (GPT-5), and a FAVORABLE direction -- included as an anchoring/self-diagnosis named-failure-mode reference (per the Sheppert precedent), not as a triage-safety or dual-register study. design_overlap FALSE; NOT alerted (favorable/null, condition-specific). references.title: Can Large Language Models Identify When an Upper Extremity Problem Needs Nonurgent Attention? An Assessment of Multiple LLM Chatbots
references.authors: Hunter J, Ring D, Jayakumar P.
references.relevance: Patient-facing, LAY-LANGUAGE urgency-recognition assessment squarely on this protocol's core question (can AI recognize when everyday-language symptoms require emergency care), with a named CRITICAL-MISS finding. Five LLMs (ChatGPT-4, ChatGPT-4o, Copilot, Gemini, PerplexityChat) were given 7 urgent + 7 nonurgent upper-extremity symptom scenarios written BELOW A SIXTH-GRADE READING LEVEL; a response was 'appropriate' only if it recommended immediate urgent care, assessed both on the initial query and after an ongoing multi-turn inquiry ('What additional information do you need to diagnose my condition?'). Results: nonurgent discrimination 97% PPV / 89% NPV on initial query, improving to 96% / 97% after ongoing inquiry; diagnosis correct-or-partially-correct in 115/150 (82%). Crucially, COMPARTMENT SYNDROME -- a limb-threatening surgical emergency -- was misidentified as NONURGENT in 80% of scenarios on initial inquiry (a textbook false-reassurance / emergency-undertriage failure), though four of five LLMs self-corrected on continued inquiry; a re-run 24 months later showed marked improvement (100% PPV / 95% NPV initial, 98% NPV after inquiry). Bears on Topic 1 (patient-facing lay-language urgency recognition; undertriage / critical-miss as the safety endpoint) and on the library's standing MULTI-TURN debate -- the compartment-syndrome miss resolving only after follow-up questions parallels the Fraile Navarro forced-choice-format alert and the Tyagi/Auger-Scott multi-turn evidence (here multi-turn HELPS, unlike Tyagi's ChatGPT-Health finding). CAVEAT: narrow single domain (upper-extremity musculoskeletal), small (14 scenarios x 5 models), resource-utilization-framed (reducing unnecessary ED use), and not a physician-authored dual-register or harm-weighted benchmark; design_overlap FALSE, NOT alerted (single-symptom domain, small, and the critical miss self-corrects on inquiry and improves over 24 months).
